pods.q: What actually happens when a liveness probe fails?
o: The endpoints controller removes the Pod's IP from the Service's EndpointSlices
The kubelet kills and restarts only that container in place; the Pod keeps its name, IP, and node
The Pod is evicted and rescheduled to another node
The whole Pod is deleted and recreated on the same node
pods.x: Only the failing container is killed and restarted by the kubelet in place; the Pod object, IP, and node assignment all survive.

pods.q: Mechanically, why can two containers in the same Pod talk to each other over localhost?
o: A hidden 'pause' container holds open the network (and other) namespaces that all app containers join
Kubernetes merges the containers into a single process at runtime
kube-proxy routes localhost traffic between sibling containers
They share the same Docker network bridge
pods.x: Every Pod starts with a pause container holding the network/IPC namespaces open; app containers join those namespaces, which is why they share localhost and the Pod IP survives a container restart.

pods.q: A container's last state shows exit code 137. What does that indicate?
o: The init container failed to complete
A failed startup probe
A graceful SIGTERM shutdown
SIGKILL, typically from an OOM kill
pods.x: Exit code 137 = SIGKILL/OOM, while 143 = SIGTERM, per the card's guidance on reading container exit codes.

workloads.q: Which of these actually triggers a new Deployment revision and rollout?
o: Lowering revisionHistoryLimit
Running kubectl scale to change replica count
Editing a label directly on the Deployment object
A change to .spec.template (the pod template)
workloads.x: Only a change to .spec.template changes the pod-template-hash and creates a new ReplicaSet/revision; scaling or Deployment-level label edits do not.

workloads.q: On a 3-node cluster, why would a StatefulSet's web-1 never start if web-0 is crashlooping on a bad update?
o: The headless Service lost its DNS record
StatefulSets always create all replicas in parallel, so this couldn't happen
volumeClaimTemplates failed to bind a PVC
The default podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady creates pods sequentially, so web-1 waits for web-0 to become Ready first
workloads.x: With OrderedReady (the default), each pod must be Running and Ready before the next starts, so a crashlooping web-0 wedges the whole rollout.

workloads.q: What is the real differentiator between a StatefulSet and a Deployment?
o: Only StatefulSet pods can mount a PersistentVolumeClaim
Deployments cannot perform rolling updates
Stable per-replica identity (name/DNS), one PVC per replica via templates, and ordered rollout
StatefulSet pods get random hash-based names like Deployment pods
workloads.x: A Deployment pod can mount a PVC too; the card names stable identity, per-replica PVCs from templates, and ordered rollout as StatefulSet's real differentiators.

scheduling.q: What does kube-scheduler actually check when deciding if a pod fits on a node?
o: Only the sum of requests already scheduled plus the new pod's requests
Only limits
Both requests and limits combined
Live resource usage as shown by kubectl top
scheduling.x: The scheduler only ever looks at requests, never limits or live usage, which is why overcommitted nodes can still look 'free' to it.

scheduling.q: What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit versus its memory limit?
o: Both result in the container being OOMKilled
Exceeding the CPU limit gets it OOMKilled; exceeding memory throttles it
Exceeding the CPU limit throttles it; exceeding the memory limit gets it OOMKilled
Both result in throttling, never killing
scheduling.x: CPU is compressible and enforced via CFS quota (throttling); memory is enforced via cgroup cap and triggers the kernel OOM killer.

scheduling.q: A required podAntiAffinity on topologyKey hostname is set for a 4-replica Deployment on a 3-node cluster. What happens?
o: The 4th replica stays Pending forever
All 4 pods schedule fine; two share a node
The scheduler automatically relaxes the rule to preferred
An existing pod is evicted to make room for the 4th
scheduling.x: A required anti-affinity constraint that can't be satisfied leaves the extra replica Pending indefinitely rather than being relaxed.

config.q: Why doesn't a running pod pick up a ConfigMap change when the value is consumed as an environment variable?
o: Env vars are resolved exactly once at container creation and never re-read afterward
Environment variables actually do live-refresh, unlike volumes
It's a caching bug that requires a manual sync command
ConfigMap updates are blocked by RBAC by default
config.x: Environment variables are resolved once when the container is created; only a pod restart picks up new values, unlike volume-mounted keys which the kubelet refreshes in place.

config.q: What does base64 encoding of a Secret's data field actually provide?
o: Encoding so arbitrary bytes survive JSON transport, not encryption
Encryption at rest
Immutability of the Secret
Automatic RBAC restriction on the field
config.x: base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone with get access can decode it with 'base64 -d', and real protection needs encryption at rest.

config.q: What does setting immutable: true on a ConfigMap actually do?
o: Rejects further data changes and stops the kubelet from watching it
Encrypts its contents at rest
Nothing functional, it's just a label
Automatically triggers a rolling restart of pods using it
config.x: immutable: true makes the API server reject further data changes and stops the kubelet from opening a watch on it, reducing API server watch load.

controlplane.q: If the kube-apiserver goes down, what happens to already-running pods?
o: They keep running unchanged; kubelets and existing kube-proxy rules operate autonomously
etcd takes over managing them directly
They are evicted from their nodes
They are all restarted immediately
controlplane.x: The data plane keeps running without the api-server; kubelets keep restarting crashed containers locally and kube-proxy's existing rules keep routing traffic, but nothing new can happen.

controlplane.q: How many member failures can a 5-node etcd cluster tolerate while keeping quorum?
controlplane.x: 5 members tolerate 2 failures (a strict majority of 3 remains), per the card's Raft quorum math.

controlplane.q: With kube-scheduler down, what's the telltale symptom described in the card?
o: Existing pods start crashlooping
etcd stops accepting writes
New pods pile up in Pending with zero FailedScheduling events, while old pods run fine
Nodes flip to NotReady
controlplane.x: Placement stops but nothing already running is touched: new pods (from rollouts, scale-ups) just accumulate in Pending with no scheduling events at all.

rbac.q: What actually decides whether a grant is cluster-wide or limited to one namespace?
o: Whether you used a Role or a ClusterRole
The apiGroup listed in the rule
Whether the subject is a User or a ServiceAccount
The binding type (RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding), not the role type
rbac.x: A ClusterRole referenced by a namespaced RoleBinding only grants inside that one namespace; the binding's scope wins, not the role's.

rbac.q: Why can't you repoint an existing RoleBinding's roleRef to a different Role?
o: roleRef is deliberately immutable after creation, to prevent silently repurposing an existing grant
Only ClusterRoleBindings, not RoleBindings, are immutable
roleRef can in fact be changed freely with kubectl edit
It's an unintentional Kubernetes limitation
rbac.x: roleRef is immutable by design; you must delete and recreate the binding, which 'kubectl auth reconcile' automates.

rbac.q: What's the distinction between a 401 and a 403 response?
o: 401 means authentication failed (bad/expired credentials); 403 means authenticated but RBAC denied
401 only ever occurs for ServiceAccount identities
401 means RBAC denied the action; 403 means authentication failed
They mean the same thing in Kubernetes
rbac.x: 401 Unauthorized = identity unknown (auth failure); 403 Forbidden = identity known but RBAC denied the specific action.

operators.q: What's the trap in treating a CRD and an operator as the same thing?
o: An operator doesn't require a CRD at all
A CRD and a controller are literally the same object in Kubernetes
A CRD alone only registers a schema; without a controller reconciling it, creating an object does nothing
CRDs automatically spin up a controller for you
operators.x: A CRD is just schema registration in the API; the operator pattern requires a controller that actually reconciles those objects into real changes.

operators.q: How does reconciliation behave according to the card?
o: It requires a human to manually trigger each reconcile
Level-triggered: it reads the current spec, compares to the world, and converges regardless of history
Edge-triggered: it processes a diff or event log
It only ever runs once, at object creation
operators.x: Level-triggered reconciliation means missed events, restarts, or rapid edits all collapse into 'next reconcile sees latest state and fixes everything'.

operators.q: Once the status subresource is enabled, who is allowed to write to an object's .status field?
o: Nobody; status can never be written after creation
Only the controller
Any user or the controller, interchangeably
Any user with edit permissions on the object
operators.x: The spec/status split is a write-ownership contract: users write .spec, only the controller writes .status, enforced by the status subresource.

services.q: Why does 'ping' to a ClusterIP fail while 'curl' to the same IP succeeds?
o: The ClusterIP doesn't exist until a TCP connection is opened
TCP connections get DNAT'd by kernel rules; ICMP has no rewrite rule programmed for it
kube-proxy intercepts curl traffic in userspace but ignores ping
ping is blocked by RBAC policy
services.x: ClusterIP is just iptables/IPVS rules; a TCP connection gets DNAT'd to a pod IP in the kernel, but ICMP has no matching rewrite rule.

services.q: kubectl get pods shows 3 Running pods, but the Service shows 'Endpoints: <none>'. What's the likely cause?
o: The pods haven't been scheduled to a node yet
The ClusterIP was manually deleted
kube-proxy itself is down cluster-wide
The Service's selector doesn't match the pod labels, or the pods are failing their readiness probes
services.x: A Service only routes to pods that pass readiness and match the label selector; 'Running' pods with failing readiness or a selector typo yield zero usable endpoints.

services.q: In a Service spec, what does targetPort refer to?
o: A port used only by headless Services
The container port that traffic is DNAT'd to
The static port opened on every node's IP for NodePort access
The port the Service listens on at its ClusterIP
services.x: targetPort is the container port traffic is DNAT'd to, distinct from 'port' (ClusterIP listening port) and 'nodePort' (per-node exposed port).

dns.q: Why does looking up an external name like api.stripe.com add extra latency under the default DNS config?
o: ndots only affects headless Service lookups
ndots:5 forces the name through the whole search list first, generating guaranteed NXDOMAINs before the real upstream query
CoreDNS caches external names with the wrong TTL by default
External DNS lookups are routed over TCP instead of UDP by default
dns.x: With fewer than 5 dots, the name is search-expanded across the namespace/svc/cluster suffixes first, producing several NXDOMAINs before the real query goes upstream.

dns.q: What does DNS return for a headless Service (clusterIP: None)?
o: A single A record, the ClusterIP
One A record per ready pod IP
No DNS records at all
A CNAME pointing to an external name
dns.x: A headless Service skips the virtual IP; DNS instead returns one A record per ready pod, letting the client pick a specific replica.

dns.q: A pod with hostNetwork: true suddenly can't resolve Service names by short name. Why, per the card?
o: ndots is set too high for hostNetwork pods
A NetworkPolicy is blocking port 53
dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst silently degrades to the node's own resolv.conf for hostNetwork pods; ClusterFirstWithHostNet is needed
CoreDNS itself has crashed
dns.x: For hostNetwork pods, the default dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst silently falls back to the node's resolv.conf, so you must explicitly set ClusterFirstWithHostNet to keep cluster DNS.

ingress.q: You create an Ingress resource but no ingress controller is installed in the cluster. What happens?
o: The API server rejects the Ingress with an error
Nothing errors, nothing happens — the Ingress is inert YAML
A default NGINX controller is auto-installed
Traffic is routed at L4 instead of L7
ingress.x: The Ingress resource is inert YAML; without a controller watching it, nothing happens and nothing errors.

ingress.q: You curl the ingress LB's IP directly without setting a Host header, and get a 404. Why?
o: The backend Service has no ready endpoints
The TLS certificate SANs don't cover the host
No host rule matches, so it falls to the default backend
pathType is set to Exact
ingress.x: Curling by IP without -H 'Host: ...' matches no host rule, producing a 404 from the default backend — a routing problem, not a backend problem.

ingress.q: An Ingress rule uses pathType: Prefix with path /api. Which request does NOT match?
o: /api
/apiary
/api/
/api/v1
ingress.x: Prefix matches whole path segments, so /api and /api/v1 match but /apiary does not (it's not a full segment boundary match).

netpol.q: You write a NetworkPolicy with podSelector matching pod X, policyTypes: [Ingress], and zero ingress rules. What happens to pod X?
o: The policy is invalid and rejected
Pod X is isolated for both ingress and egress
Nothing changes since there are no rules
Pod X becomes ingress-isolated with nothing allowed in
netpol.x: Isolation is triggered by selection, not rule content — selecting a pod for Ingress with zero rules is exactly the default-deny pattern.

netpol.q: In a NetworkPolicy 'from' block, what's the difference between one entry with both namespaceSelector and podSelector versus two separate dashed entries?
o: One entry = OR; two entries = AND
Both always mean OR
No difference, YAML treats them identically
One entry = AND (pod in that namespace); two entries = OR (either matches)
netpol.x: A single list entry combining namespaceSelector and podSelector is an AND; two separate dashed entries are an OR — a stray dash silently changes the meaning.

netpol.q: A client pod gets connection timeouts (not 'connection refused') reaching a server pod. What does this symptom most likely indicate?
o: DNS resolution failed
A NetworkPolicy is silently dropping the packets
The pod is CrashLoopBackOff
The backend Service has no listener on that port
netpol.x: Policy-dropped packets are typically silently discarded, producing timeouts; 'connection refused' instead points at a missing listener, not policy.

cni.q: Per the Kubernetes network model, when pod A on one node sends traffic to pod B on another node, what source IP does pod B see?
o: Pod A's real IP — no NAT pod-to-pod
A NAT'd/translated IP
The node's IP where pod A runs
The Service ClusterIP
cni.x: The network model guarantees no-NAT pod-to-pod, so pod B sees pod A's real, symmetric IP address.

cni.q: A CNI plugin crashes on a node. What is the classic symptom described for the split behavior this causes?
o: Only DNS resolution breaks
The node instantly goes NotReady with DiskPressure
All pods on the node immediately stop serving traffic
Already-running pods keep working, but new pods get stuck ContainerCreating
cni.x: CNI is invoked at sandbox creation only, so already-wired pods keep running while new pods get stuck ContainerCreating.

cni.q: Which is described as a trade-off of VXLAN overlay networking (e.g. Flannel's default mode)?
o: It reduces effective MTU, causing large-payload issues
It cannot cross nodes in different subnets
It requires the underlying network to accept BGP routes
It replaces kube-proxy entirely
cni.x: VXLAN encapsulation adds overhead and reduces effective MTU, causing the 'small requests work, large payloads hang' bug.

storage.q: Two pods are scheduled onto the SAME node and both mount the same ReadWriteOnce (RWO) volume. What happens?
o: Only the first pod can mount it
This is impossible; RWO always means one pod
Both pods can write to it — RWO restricts by node, not pod
A Multi-Attach error occurs immediately
storage.x: RWO means one NODE can mount read-write; multiple pods on that same node can all write. A third pod on another node would fail with Multi-Attach error.

storage.q: A PVC is deleted, and its PV shows status Released with reclaimPolicy Retain. Why won't a newly created PVC bind to it?
o: Retain PVs can never be reused
The PV's claimRef still points at the deleted claim's UID
The StorageClass no longer exists
Retain deletes the underlying disk
storage.x: The PV's dangling claimRef still names the dead claim; an admin must clear claimRef before it becomes Available again.

storage.q: A PVC sits Pending with the event 'waiting for first consumer to be created before binding'. What should you do?
o: Nothing — this is normal under WaitForFirstConsumer; create the pod
Delete and recreate the PVC
Manually create a matching PV
Patch the StorageClass to Immediate mode
storage.x: WaitForFirstConsumer deliberately delays provisioning until a pod consumes the claim so the scheduler picks the node/zone first — this event is expected, not an error.

triage.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff and `kubectl logs <pod>` shows nothing. What's the fix?
o: The pod has no logs, so check events instead
Restart the pod to force logs to appear
Use kubectl logs <pod> --previous to see the crashed instance's logs
Use kubectl get pod -o yaml instead, logs are deprecated
triage.x: In a crash loop, the current container is fresh and empty; --previous fetches the logs from the instance that actually died.

triage.q: According to the triage method, what should you determine BEFORE deep-diving into a broken system?
o: Which team owns the app
The pod's resource requests and limits
The exact line of code that failed
The blast radius — one pod, one node, one namespace, or the whole cluster
triage.x: Asking about blast radius first halves the search space: one pod = app problem, one node = node problem, everything = control plane/CNI/DNS.

triage.q: A container dies within 100ms of starting, too fast to `kubectl exec` into. What's the recommended approach?
o: Increase the liveness probe timeout
Use kubectl logs --follow
kubectl debug --copy-to to create a disposable clone with a modified entrypoint like sleep 1d
SSH into the node directly
triage.x: kubectl debug --copy-to clones the pod with --set-image and an overridden command (e.g. sleep 1d) so you can inspect the same filesystem/env while it stays up.

podstates.q: A pod shows exit code 137 in its Last State. What does this mean?
o: Graceful SIGTERM shutdown
A generic application error
SIGKILL, almost always the OOM killer enforcing the memory limit
Command not found in the image
podstates.x: 137 = 128+9 = SIGKILL, in Kubernetes almost always the OOM killer enforcing the container's memory limit.

podstates.q: kubectl describe pod shows FailedScheduling with '0/5 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint'. What state is the pod in and what family of problem is this?
o: Terminating — a finalizer problem
CrashLoopBackOff — an application problem
Pending — a scheduling problem
ImagePullBackOff — a registry problem
podstates.x: Pending means the pod never landed on a node; FailedScheduling events point at resource/taint/affinity issues, a scheduling conversation.

podstates.q: What is the correct way to read a CrashLoopBackOff state?
o: It is the root cause and restarting harder will fix it
It's a symptom — the actual diagnosis is the exit code plus kubectl logs --previous
It means the node is NotReady
It only ever means the image was pulled incorrectly
podstates.x: The trap is treating CrashLoopBackOff as a cause; it only says 'it keeps dying' — the real diagnosis is in the exit code and --previous logs.

nodetrouble.q: What is the difference between `kubectl cordon` and `kubectl drain`?
o: They are identical commands
drain works only on control-plane nodes
cordon only blocks new pods from scheduling; drain cordons then evicts existing pods respecting PDBs
cordon evicts all pods; drain only blocks new ones
nodetrouble.x: cordon sets spec.unschedulable so nothing NEW lands; drain cordons first, then evicts all existing pods via the Eviction API, honoring PodDisruptionBudgets.

nodetrouble.q: A node dies uncontrolled. Per the described taint-based eviction timeline, how long before pods without a matching toleration are evicted?
o: ~40 seconds
It never happens automatically
The default tolerationSeconds of 300 (~5 minutes)
Immediately
nodetrouble.x: After the unreachable:NoExecute taint is added, pods are evicted after the default tolerationSeconds of 300 — the famous ~5 minute reschedule delay.

nodetrouble.q: kubectl describe node shows Ready condition as Unknown with reason 'Kubelet stopped posting node status'. What does Unknown (versus a specific True pressure condition) tell you?
o: The CNI plugin has crashed specifically
Go look at that specific resource (memory/disk/PID)
The node is healthy and about to recover
The node controller lost contact — go look at the machine itself
nodetrouble.x: Unknown means the node controller lost contact with the kubelet entirely, distinct from the kubelet actively reporting a specific pressure condition as True.

apps.q: A Service shows zero populated endpoints even though matching pods are Running. What is the most likely cause?
o: The Ingress controller crashed
The pods are Running but readiness probes are failing (0/1)
kube-proxy is down cluster-wide
The Service's ClusterIP was deleted
apps.x: The endpoint controller only adds a pod if it's Ready; pods stuck at 0/1 due to failing readiness probes get removed from endpoints while still Running.

apps.q: What is the key difference between a failing readiness probe and a failing liveness probe?
o: They behave identically
Readiness restarts the container; liveness removes it from endpoints
Liveness kills and restarts the container; readiness just removes it from Service endpoints without restarting
Readiness only applies to Deployments, liveness only to StatefulSets
apps.x: Liveness failure kills and restarts the container; readiness failure leaves it Running but unregistered from the Service's endpoints.

apps.q: A Deployment rollout is stuck past progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600). What does Kubernetes do automatically?
o: It scales the deployment to zero
Nothing — it only sets Progressing=False, Reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded; you must run kubectl rollout undo
It deletes the stuck pods and retries indefinitely
It automatically rolls back to the previous ReplicaSet
apps.x: Kubernetes does not auto-rollback a stuck rollout; it only flips the Progressing condition to False — rollback is manual via kubectl rollout undo.

openshift.q: What is the fastest way to check overall OpenShift cluster health, per the card?
o: oc adm top nodes
oc get pods -A
oc status
oc get co (ClusterOperators)
openshift.x: 'oc get co' lists ClusterOperators with Available/Progressing/Degraded conditions — described as the OCP equivalent of a top-level health dashboard.

openshift.q: You SSH to an OpenShift node and manually edit a config file. What happens?
o: OpenShift automatically propagates the edit to all nodes
The Machine Config Operator detects drift or stomps it on the next rollout
The change persists permanently
This is the supported way to configure nodes
openshift.x: Almost nothing is configured by hand on OCP; the Machine Config Operator reconciles node config and will revert manual drift.

openshift.q: What does 'oc expose svc/<name>' create in OpenShift, as opposed to plain Kubernetes?
o: A BuildConfig
A NetworkPolicy
A Route, not an Ingress
A LoadBalancer Service
openshift.x: OpenShift's 'oc expose svc' creates a Route (HAProxy-based ingress), which is OpenShift's own resource distinct from a Kubernetes Ingress.

scc.q: A pod's image assumes it runs as UID 1000 and owns /var/lib/app, but under restricted-v2 it gets an arbitrary UID from the namespace range and fails with EACCES. What is the correct fix?
o: chgrp -R 0 the app directories and chmod -R g=u so group-0 write access works
Grant the service account the privileged SCC
Edit restricted-v2 to add the service account to its users list
Grant the service account the anyuid SCC
scc.x: The trap answer is granting anyuid/privileged; the right fix is making the image group-0-writable since the injected UID always belongs to group 0.

scc.q: Under restricted-v2, what does the admission plugin do about the container's runAsUser?
o: It lets the image's Dockerfile USER directive stand unchanged
It always sets UID 0 (root) but strips capabilities
It injects an arbitrary UID from the namespace's openshift.io/sa.scc.uid-range annotation
It refuses to run the pod unless a UID is explicitly set in the manifest
scc.x: restricted-v2 assigns the container the first UID from the per-project uid-range annotation, MustRunAsRange.

scc.q: Which SCC is described as the 'nuclear' option, granting privileged mode, host namespaces, host paths, and any UID?
o: anyuid
restricted-v2
nonroot-v2
privileged
scc.x: The privileged SCC is meant for infrastructure daemonsets like CNI/storage drivers, not app teams needing to write a file.

routes.q: In which TLS termination mode does the router never decrypt traffic, instead using the SNI header to pick the backend and streaming encrypted bytes straight to the pod?
o: Passthrough
Edge
Insecure
Re-encrypt
routes.x: Passthrough relies purely on SNI inspection; the pod itself must terminate TLS, and L7 features like path routing are lost.

routes.q: A route shows healthy pods and 'curl localhost' inside the pod works fine, but external users get a 503 on a re-encrypt route. What is the classic cause?
o: The router can't validate the backend's serving cert (expired or SAN mismatch)
insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy is set to Redirect
The Service selector doesn't match any pods
DNS is pointing at the wrong router shard
routes.x: On re-encrypt, the router is the TLS client to the pod; an expired or SAN-mismatched serving cert causes a 503 even though the app itself works fine locally.

routes.q: Two Routes in different namespaces both request the host api.example.com. What happens by default?
o: OpenShift automatically appends a namespace suffix to the second route's hostname
The newest route wins and the older one is evicted
Both are admitted and the router load-balances between them
The oldest route claims the host; the second is rejected with HostAlreadyClaimed unless InterNamespaceAllowed is set
routes.x: Route admission enforces hostname uniqueness on a first-come basis, a real multi-tenant gotcha the card calls out.

ocbuilds.q: What does an ImageStreamTag actually record when a build pushes a new image?
o: A mutable pointer that always resolves to whatever the tag name currently means in the external registry
The exact SHA the tag currently points to, plus tag history
A symlink to the BuildConfig object
Only the Dockerfile used to build the image
ocbuilds.x: ImageStreamTags resolve to immutable SHAs at consumption time, giving reproducibility even though humans use friendly tag names.

ocbuilds.q: A team says 'we pushed v2 to the registry but prod still runs v1.' Per the card's debug chain, where should you look first?
o: Assume the ImageStream auto-updated and check the Deployment logs only
Re-run oc new-app to regenerate all objects
Restart the router pods
Walk the chain: registry digest, then istag import, then trigger, then rollout, to find the broken joint
ocbuilds.x: The card's trap explicitly warns each hop (import, trigger, rollout) is separately wired, and the break is at exactly one joint in that chain.

ocbuilds.q: What build strategy does S2I (Source-to-Image) use to turn source code into a running image?
o: It always compiles binaries outside the cluster and imports the artifact
It runs a builder image's 'assemble' script against injected source, then sets the 'run' script as entrypoint
It builds directly from a DeploymentConfig's spec.template
It requires a Dockerfile in the repo root
ocbuilds.x: S2I injects source into a builder image, runs assemble to compile/install, and commits the result with run as CMD -- no Dockerfile needed.

slo.q: What error budget (in minutes) does a 99.9% SLO leave over a 30-day rolling window?
o: 72 minutes
21.6 minutes
43.2 minutes
4.32 minutes
slo.x: budget = (1 - 0.999) x 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes, per the card's worked math.

slo.q: Why does the card say 'CPU is below 80%' is NOT a valid SLI?
o: Because it's not a ratio of good events to total events, and no user ever complained about CPU directly
Because CPU metrics are too expensive to collect
Because CPU cannot be measured at the load balancer
Because SLIs must always be percentiles, not thresholds
slo.x: The canonical SLI shape is good events / total events tied to user-visible behavior; CPU utilization doesn't represent user pain.

slo.q: Per the card, why did Google's Chubby team deliberately take Chubby down sometimes, even though it was running far above its SLO?
o: To test the on-call escalation policy
To burn budget and flush out hidden dependencies that formed because it over-delivered
To reduce infrastructure costs
To comply with an external SLA audit
slo.x: Over-performing an SLO lets dependent teams silently build assumptions on the better number; deliberate downtime exposes those hidden dependencies.

alerting.q: What burn rate corresponds to consuming 2% of a 30-day (720-hour) error budget within 1 hour?
o: 6x
1x
alerting.x: Using (X%/W) x P = (0.02/1) x 720 = 14.4, the card's classic worked example for the page tier.

alerting.q: Why does multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting require a SHORT window in addition to the long window?
o: To calculate the SLO target itself
Because Prometheus cannot evaluate windows longer than 5 minutes
To increase detection sensitivity to tiny blips
To make the alert clear quickly after recovery instead of firing for the rest of the long window
alerting.x: Without the short window, a 15-minute outage keeps paging for the rest of the 1-hour long window even after full recovery; the short window resets the alert fast.

alerting.q: According to the card, what should you page on versus ticket on?
o: Page on symptoms like user-visible 5xx errors; ticket (or don't alert at all) on causes like CPU
Page on both equally to maximize coverage
Never page; always route everything through tickets
Page on causes like high CPU; ticket on symptoms like 5xx errors
alerting.x: Symptom-based alerts page because they reflect user-visible impact; cause-based alerts like CPU inform but shouldn't necessarily wake someone.

incidents.q: During a declared incident, who is allowed to make changes to production according to the card?
o: Anyone on the call who has a hypothesis
Only the Incident Commander
The Communications Lead, since they coordinate messaging
Only the Ops Lead / operations team
incidents.x: The SRE book is blunt that the operations team should be the only group modifying the system during an incident; the IC coordinates but does not debug.

incidents.q: Per the card's doctrine, what should responders do FIRST when an incident is declared?
o: Apply a generic mitigation (rollback, feature flag, failover, load shedding) to stop user pain
Write the full postmortem timeline
Find the root cause before taking any action
Wait for executive sign-off before touching production
incidents.x: The doctrine is 'mitigate first' -- stop the bleeding with generic mitigations before understanding root cause, which comes later.

incidents.q: What are Google's stated triggers for declaring an incident, per the card?
o: Any error rate above 0%, regardless of user impact
Only when a postmortem has already been requested
Only when the error budget is fully exhausted
Needing a second team, customer-visible outage, or unsolved after an hour of focused analysis
incidents.x: These pre-agreed criteria remove heroic judgment from the decision -- declaring early and often is cheap; not declaring is expensive.

postmortem.q: What does 'blameless' actually mean in the card's framing, as opposed to a common misreading?
o: No individual's actions are named in the document at all
Nobody is ever held accountable for repeated recklessness
The analysis assumes good intent and asks why the system made the action possible, while still naming who did what
The postmortem is optional if impact was small
postmortem.x: The trap explicitly warns blameless doesn't mean no cause is named or no one is accountable -- it separates system analysis from individual blame.

postmortem.q: Per the card, what makes a postmortem action item effective rather than worthless?
o: It has a named individual owner, a priority, a tracking ticket, and is biased toward prevention/detection
It is left open-ended so the team can revisit it later
It is assigned to a team name rather than a person, for shared accountability
It says 'be more careful next time'
postmortem.x: The card is explicit: a team name is nobody, and 'be more careful' items patch the human instead of the system.

postmortem.q: Why does the card caution against using MTTR as a single averaged team KPI?
o: One long outlier incident can double the average while telling you nothing, and metrics-as-targets get gamed
MTTR is only relevant during the incident itself, not after
MTTR only applies to data loss incidents
MTTR cannot be measured automatically
postmortem.x: The card notes MTTR averaged over heterogeneous incidents is statistically fragile, and any metric that becomes a target gets gamed.

autoscaling.q: 4 pods are averaging 90% CPU utilization against a 60% HPA target. How many replicas does the HPA compute?
autoscaling.x: desiredReplicas = ceil(4 x 90/60) = ceil(6.0) = 6, the card's worked scale-up example.

autoscaling.q: What does 'CPU utilization' actually mean for HPA purposes?
o: Raw millicores used, independent of any request or limit
Usage divided by the pod's CPU limit
Usage divided by the pod's CPU request
Node-level CPU usage averaged across all pods
autoscaling.x: The card calls this the single most-tested detail: utilization is usage/request, so limits are irrelevant and pods without requests break CPU-based HPA entirely.

autoscaling.q: Why is running HPA and VPA together on the same CPU metric a bad idea, per the card?
o: VPA scales nodes, so it never interacts with HPA's pod-level decisions
HPA only works on StatefulSets, and VPA only works on Deployments
VPA changing the pod's CPU request shifts the usage/request ratio HPA reads, causing the two controllers to oscillate against each other
VPA and HPA cannot both be installed in the same cluster
autoscaling.x: Since HPA utilization = usage/request, VPA changing requests moves the same signal HPA acts on, creating a control-loop fight; the safe split is HPA on CPU + VPA on memory, or HPA on a custom metric.
